BEFORE THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION 

In the Matter of:

O R D E R 
Every year each electric utility files its Reliability Report and Vegetation 
Management Update in this matter.1 Duke Kentucky Energy, Inc. (Duke Kentucky) has 
filed petitions annually,2 pursuant to 807 KAR 5:001, Section 13, and KRS 61.878, 
requesting that the Commission grant confidential treatment for an indefinite period for 
the physical addresses of its substations and circuits.3 
In support of its petitions, Duke Kentucky argued that the information, if openly 
disclosed, could present security and safety issues by identifying locations of critical utility 
infrastructure that would unnecessarily expose the public to potential harm if exploited.4

Duke Kentucky claimed that disclosure of this information could result in possible security 
issues such as including theft, destruction, possible injury, and vandalism.5 
Having considered the petitions and the material at issue, the Commission finds 
that disclosure of the physical addresses of utility infrastructure would result in 
compromising infrastructure security and as such is generally recognized as confidential; 
it therefore meets the criteria for confidential treatment and should be exempted from 
public disclosure pursuant to 807 KAR 5:001, Section 13, and KRS 61.878(1)(m). 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that: 
1. 
Duke Kentucky’s April 28, 2026 petition for confidential treatment is granted. 
2.

3.

not be placed in the public record or made available for public inspection for an indefinite

6.

in any Commission proceeding shall comply with 807 KAR 5:001, Section 13(9). 
7.

Blockware Mining, LLC (Blockware). The information is filed yearly with the Commission

requires that all public records “be open for inspection by any person, except as otherwise

title: KY PSC Order — Case No. 2020-00019: ELECTRONIC APPLICATION OF KENTUCKY POWER COMPANY FOR APPROVAL OF A CONTRACT FOR ELECTRIC SERVICE WITH AIR PRODUCTS AND CHEMICALS, INC

On April 1, 2024, Kentucky Power Company (Kentucky Power) filed a motion, 
pursuant to 807 KAR 5:001, Section 13, and KRS 61.878, requesting that the Commission 
grant confidential treatment for ten years for portions of Kentucky Power’s annual report 
of revenues received from and marginal costs of providing service to Air Products and 
Chemicals (Air Products) under the terms of a special contract. The designated material 
consists of customer-specific billing information. 
Kentucky Power requested confidential treatment of the designated material 
pursuant to KRS 61.878(1)(c)(1), which prohibits public disclosure of material that is 
confidential or proprietary and, if publicly disclosed, would result in unfair commercial 
advantage. 
In support of its motion, Kentucky Power asserted that Air Products expects 
Kentucky Power to protect the confidentiality of the information. Kentucky Power 
explained that Air Products operates in a competitive national market and that public 
disclosure of the designated material would provide Air Products’ competitors with an 
unfair commercial advantage. Kentucky Power contended that, as a result of public 
disclosure of confidential information that could result in a commercial disadvantage, 

-2-
Case No. 2020-00019 
other commercial and industrial customers would be less likely to locate their businesses 
in Kentucky Power’s service territory, which would result in harm to Kentucky Power and 
its customers from a declining customer base. Kentucky Power stated that the 
Commission granted confidential treatment to the same information previously filed in this 
case in an Order issued on April 8, 2021.1 
Having considered the motion and the material at issue, the Commission finds that 
the designated material is generally recognized as confidential or proprietary because 
public disclosure could ultimately result in an unfair commercial advantage to Kentucky 
Power’s competitors. This is because public disclosure of information that impacts a utility 
customer’s position in the marketplace could result in businesses being less likely to 
locate in the utility’s service territory. Kentucky Power files this information on an annual 
basis pursuant to an April 23, 2020 Order entered in this proceeding.2 The Commission 
notes that it granted confidential treatment to the same information contained in Kentucky 
Power’s annual filings in Orders dated April 8, 2021,3 March 16, 2022,4 and August 8, 
2023.5 Additionally, KRS 278.160(3) allows for confidential treatment for provisions of a 
special contract that otherwise would be exempt from public disclosure under 
KRS 61.878(1)(c)(1). For these reasons, the Commission finds that the designated 
material meets the criteria for confidential treatment and should be exempted from public 
disclosure pursuant to 807 KAR 5:001, Section 13, and KRS 61.878(1)(c)(1) for ten years.

regarding Martin District’s lack of capable management, and proposed a "structured path" 
with Martin District contracting with a third party to manage and operate the utility in order 
to prevent Martin District's collapse and return Martin District to solid financial and 
managerial footing.63 Martin District has complied with the Commission’s directive in that 
2018 case, and operated under the Management Contract with Alliance since 2021. In 
its motion, Martin District asserted that, since that time, it has made improvements and 
there is every reason to believe that it will continue to improve under its new leadership.64 
The Commission acknowledges Martin District’s recent efforts under the current 
management and with Alliance to improve the system, including actions such as obtaining 
additional revenue and prosecuting water theft. This order should not be construed to 
take anything away from the hard work that has been undertaken by Martin District. 
However, the past financial and management crises in the district placed it in a dire 
situation and presented Martin District and Alliance with a monumental task that is 
incomplete at this time. While improvements have been made, it appears those have

Having considered the motion and the evidence, the Commission finds Martin 
District’s motion should be denied. As discussed above, absent Alliance, Martin District 
has not provided sufficient evidence that it is able to fulfill its statutory obligations without 
a third-party management company. The Commission ordered Martin District to collect 
the Management/Infrastructure Surcharge until a final Order is entered in its next rate 
case or until the Management Contract with Alliance expires, whichever occurs first, or 
upon further Order by this Commission.66 Martin District has not met either of the initial 
conditions; it has not filed for any adjustment of rates since 2021,67 it has asserted it is 
not seeking a rate increase at this time,68 and its contract with Alliance has been extended 
through December 31, 2029.69 As noted, the Commission has not been presented with 
sufficient evidence that Martin District be relieved of this directive. 
Further, Martin District is still collecting both the Debt Service Surcharge and 
Management/Infrastructure surcharge as part of its current rates.70 Martin District argued 
in its Motion that the July 22, 2020 Order ”did not specify how long it would last or what

As an initial matter, the Commission would note the span of time and severity of 
the issues in Martin District resulted from decades of mismanagement, and have required 
examination and remedial measures through multiple proceedings with the 
Commission.72 While the Commission commends the work Martin District has 
undertaken, the Commission would be remiss in its statutory authority to ensure Martin 
District’s customers are provided safe, reliable and adequate water service if Martin 
District were prematurely relieved of oversight for its acknowledged continuing issues. 
Further, the Commission did set forth terms in the previous Orders related to Martin 
District that were goal and accountability related; for example, the conditions discussed 
above. The Commission actively monitors collection of surcharges granted to utilities, 
and monthly and quarterly reports are required as a condition of those surcharges. The 
Commission wants to ensure transparency and oversight when customers are required 
to pay an additional charge in order to assist a utility to comply with its obligations set 
forth in KRS 278.030. Accordingly, the Commission finds that so long as Martin District 
is collecting its Debt Service Surcharge or its Management/Infrastructure Surcharge, this 
case shall remain active and the reporting requirements set forth in the July 22, 2020

infrastructure work is still needed to the system, the Commission further finds that Martin 
District and Alliance should prepare an updated infrastructure plan within 120 days to 
provide the Commission with the current status of any continued and new issues in the 
system and any plans for infrastructure improvements to assist with decreasing 
unaccounted-for water loss.

issued February 6, 2025, shall remain in effect.

2020 Order and subsequent Orders in this proceeding remain in effect. 
4. 
Martin District and Alliance shall file an updated infrastructure plan within 
120 days, providing the current status of any continued and new issues in the system and 
any plans for infrastructure improvements to assist with decreasing unaccounted-for
